title: Build a Link Shortener
summary: Design Tinylane end to end, interview style: requirements, estimates, API, key generation, storage, a cached redirect path and async click analytics.

goals.text: Turn a vague prompt into requirements and numbers
Generate short codes that never collide
Make redirects fast with a cache and an edge CDN
Keep analytics off the redirect path
Name the bottlenecks and how the design bends

steps.title: Pin down what we're building
body: The prompt: “Design a URL shortener.” Before drawing anything, agree on scope. Tinylane turns long campaign URLs into tnyl.co/xxxxxxx and redirects anyone who clicks.

Must-haves: create a short link, redirect quickly, never break a link. Nice-to-haves: custom aliases, expiry dates, click counts. Equally important are the non-functional ones: redirects must be fast and always available, and codes must not be guessable in sequence.

callout.text: Spend the first few minutes on requirements. Every later choice is justified by one of them.

card.title: Requirements
lines: # codes unique and not guessable in order

steps.title: Rough numbers
body: Assume 100 million new links a month: about 40 writes a second. If each link is clicked about 100 times, that's roughly 4,000 redirects a second, and maybe 20,000 at peak.

Over five years that's 6 billion links. At ~500 bytes each, about 3 TB: big for one machine's RAM, small for a database cluster. And 7 base62 characters (a–z, A–Z, 0–9) give 3.5 trillion codes, far more than we'll ever need.
The headline: this system is read-heavy, 100 : 1. Optimize the redirect.

steps.title: Two endpoints
body: Creating a link is a POST with the long URL and optional alias and expiry. Following one is a plain GET /{code} answered with a redirect.

Which redirect? A 301 (permanent) gets cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach us: cheaper, but we can't count them, change the target, or expire the link. A 302 (temporary) keeps every click visible. Tinylane picks 302.

steps.title: First sketch of the system
body: Behind a load balancer, split the two paths: a small Create service for writes and a larger, stateless Redirect service for reads, so each scales on its own.
The data is one key mapping to one row, with no joins, so a replicated key-value store partitioned by code fits well: every lookup goes to exactly one partition, and adding nodes adds capacity.
Every click still goes all the way to the store: about 90 ms for a user far from our region.
changes: + Load balancer, Create and Redirect services

card.title: Data model
lines: = one key in, one row out: no joins
→ a key-value store, partitioned by code

steps.title: Deep dive: why not hash the URL?
body: Tempting: take md5(long_url), base62-encode it, keep 7 characters. But 7 characters is a small space for a hash. By the birthday paradox, there's a 50% chance of a clash after only ~2.2 million links, and at 6 billion we'd expect about 5 million clashes.
So every create must first read “is this code taken?”, rehash with a salt if so, and still risk two servers claiming the same code at the same moment.

callout.text: Truncated hashes collide long before the space looks full. Collisions grow with the square of the number of links.

card.title: Hashing collides
lines: ! 50% chance of a clash by ~2.2 M links
! at 6 B links: ~5 M clashes expected
! each write: read first, retry with salt
! two servers can still race on one code

steps.title: Counters, leased in blocks
body: Instead, give every link a number that's unique by construction, then base62-encode it. A single global counter would be a bottleneck, so a tiny Range service leases each create server a block of a million ids. The server hands them out from memory and comes back once per block.

Starting at 62⁶ makes every code exactly 7 characters. To avoid codes that reveal volume or can be walked in order, pass the id through a keyed, reversible permutation first: it stays unique, but looks random.

callout.text: If a server crashes mid-block, the rest of that block is simply never used. Gaps are fine; duplicates are not.

changes: ~ Create service encodes ids in base62

card.title: Counter → base62
lines: each create server leases **1 M ids** at a time
# a crash just skips the rest of a lease

steps.title: Deep dive: the redirect path
body: Clicks are heavily skewed: a small share of fresh, popular links gets most of the traffic. A Redis cache in front of the store (cache-aside: read Redis, on a miss read the store and fill Redis) serves about 90% of lookups from a 20 GB hot set.
Store lookups fall from 4,000 to about 400 a second. Unknown codes from scanners get cached too, as short-lived “not found” entries, so they don't hammer the store.
changes: + Redis cache between Redirect service and store

steps.title: Answer at the edge
body: The remaining time is mostly distance. Putting a CDN in front lets an edge server near the clicker answer popular redirects itself: the 302 carries Cache-Control: max-age=300, so the edge reuses it for five minutes.
A hit now takes under 20 ms anywhere in the world, and the Redirect fleet shrinks from eight servers to four. The cost: an expired or edited link can live on at the edge for up to five minutes.
changes: + Edge CDN in front of the load balancer

steps.title: Count clicks without slowing them
body: Counting clicks must never delay a redirect. The Redirect service fires a small click event into a log like Kafka and responds immediately. Edge hits never reach us, so the CDN's access logs are streamed into the same topic.
A click counter consumes the events, adds them up per link per minute, and writes the totals to a stats store. Dashboards lag by about a minute, which the requirements allowed.

callout.text: Anything that isn't needed to answer the request belongs after the response: queue it.

changes: + Click counter worker and stats store
+ CDN logs feed the same topic

steps.title: Where it bends
body: Finish by stress-testing your own design. A viral link becomes one very hot key, but the edge absorbs it. If the Range service goes down, each create server still holds a lease that lasts about 21 hours at current rates. If a cache node dies, misses spike, so collapse duplicate misses into one store read.
Then the parts people forget: rate-limit link creation and scan target URLs for malware, and enforce expiry on read with a nightly sweep to delete dead rows.
changes: + Notes on range, cache and abuse risks

card.title: Where it bends
lines: ! one viral link → one hot key: the edge absorbs it
! range service down → servers keep their leases
! cache node lost → coalesce misses, warm replica
! spam & malware → rate-limit creates, scan URLs
! expiry → check expires_at on read, sweep nightly

steps.title: Tinylane, end to end
body:
• Requirements and estimates first: 40 writes/s vs 4,000 reads/s decides everything.
  • 302 over 301 keeps clicks visible and links editable.
  • Leased counter ranges + base62 give unique 7-char codes with no coordination per write; a keyed permutation hides the order.
  • Key-value store partitioned by code, replicated 3×.
  • Cache + CDN serve the hot set; the store sees a trickle.
  • Analytics are async: events after the response, counted in the background.
